summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing in Guatemalan law criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 of the victims saying they intended to flee the country.

Guatemalan officials have excluded trans women from the protection of the country's femicide legislation, justifying the exclusion on the stated ground that trans women are not "biological women". Central American governments have long maintained that exclusion, and it underpins the documented violence context for trans people in Guatemala.

There is no legal gender recognition in Guatemalan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' 2017 Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 requires states to provide legal gender recognition and marriage equality, and Guatemala was among the Latin American countries urged in January 2018 to abide by it. Compliance by Guatemala is not recorded in the available material.

Legislative activity runs against trans rights rather than toward them. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 on an anti-trans bill in Guatemala that threatened rights, including provisions that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Detention carries a specific, documented risk. Human Rights Watch's October 2020 report, which examines violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador, includes a Guatemala chapter finding that trans women are held in men's prisons on the basis of birth sex, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. Bárbara Herrarte, a trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." Lambda also flags forced internal displacement arising from violence.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a well-organised opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is generating backlash in all four countries. That regional mobilisation is the backdrop against which Guatemala's January 2022 anti-trans bill must be read.

Regional comparison is close at hand: the same Human Rights Watch investigation that documents Guatemalan prison conditions was focused on El Salvador, and Central American governments generally share the official position excluding trans women from femicide protections.

Reporting on the Inter-American Court opinion comes from regional press coverage and foundation analysis rather than from Guatemalan official sources, which is how the assessment of compliance has been assembled.
localsOnly:
Guatemalan trans residents have no route to legal gender recognition: no statute provides it, and the Inter-American Court's advisory opinion, which would compel it, has no recorded compliance in Guatemala.

Residents held in the criminal justice system are assigned to men's prisons on birth sex as of the 2020 documentation, with the sexual-assault exposure Herrarte describes and no placement policy, trans-specific unit, or court ruling on trans custody to mitigate it.

Advocacy capacity exists on the ground. Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans) and Asociación Lambda document violence, operate an observatory recording killings and day-to-day cases, and flag forced internal displacement of affected people.

The femicide-law exclusion is a matter of official Guatemalan reasoning, not an oversight in the statute: officials have stated the reasoning publicly.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Guatemala has implemented Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 is unresolved in the sources available here; January 2018 coverage records that Guatemala was urged to abide by it, and no later compliance record is sourced.

The fate of the January 2022 anti-trans bill, including whether it was enacted, amended or defeated, is not sourced in this inventory.

Not sourced in this inventory: entry and visa rules for trans travellers, document and marker requirements at Guatemalan border control, airport or security screening practices, hate-crime protection and its enforcement, restroom and facility access, healthcare or hormone access, and recognition of partners or marriages. These remain open questions rather than findings.

The 2022 violence figures come from a civil-society observatory rather than Guatemalan state statistics, and no official counter-figure is available here.
